transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Doc. Thanks for seeing me. Man, where do I even start? I guess... well, I'm a construction manager, right? Been doing this kind of work since I got out of high school, worked my way up from the bottom. It's a high-stress gig, lots of moving parts, constantly putting out fires. But what really brings me in today is... well, take a safety briefing, for example. Or like, a big plan review with the architects and the foremen. I go into the site trailer, I sit down, and I am trying *so* hard to pay attention. I tell myself, "Listen to every word, this is critical." 

But I swear, within minutes—sometimes less—my mind is just completely gone. It's off on, like, three other job problems. I'll be sitting there staring right at the guy talking, but in my head, I'm worrying about whether the concrete trucks are going to get backed up at the gate, or if the drywallers actually showed up on the second floor, or the framing issue we had last Tuesday. And because I'm miles away in my own head, I end up missing things. Important things that I *know* I should have caught in the plans or the safety protocols. And on a job site, you know, you really can't afford to miss that stuff because it costs money or someone gets hurt. It's just... it's really starting to mess with my work, and I just can't seem to keep my head in the room, no matter how hard I try to force myself to just sit and listen.
Thinking back, would you say you've had this kind of trouble staying focused since you were a kid, or is this something that started more recently, say in the past several months?

Oh, man, it's definitely not a recent thing. Not at all. If I really think back on it, it’s been this way pretty much my whole life, as far back as I can remember. I mean, we're talking way back in elementary school. I remember my parents having to go in for parent-teacher conferences all the time, and it was always the same story. The teachers would sit them down and say, "He's a smart kid, but he just cannot stay in his seat." I was always up and wandering around the classroom, or I’d be talking out of turn, blurting things out before the teacher even finished asking the question. 

And the homework—don't even get me started on the homework. I lost it constantly. I’d do it, shove it in my backpack, and then it would just disappear into this black hole of crumpled papers and old permission slips, and I could never find it when it was time to turn it in. Or if I did turn it in, it was a mess because I’d just rush through the directions. I’d see the first part of what I was supposed to do, think I had it all figured out, and just start going as fast as I could without actually reading or understanding the whole thing. So I’d end up doing the whole assignment wrong, or missing half the questions. It was just chaos, honestly. My parents tried everything—charts, rewards, punishments—but I just couldn't seem to get a grip on it. So yeah, this isn't some new stress from the job site. It’s like my brain has just always been wired this way, always going a million miles an hour and missing the details right in front of me.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of significant inattention (mind wandering during meetings, missing critical details, difficulty sustaining attention, losing items, careless errors from rushing) combined with childhood hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (out of seat, wandering classroom, blurting out answers). Symptoms are pervasive across settings (school in childhood, current workplace), have caused chronic functional impairment (academic difficulties in youth, occupational risk/errors now), and are not better explained by an acute stressor or other psychiatric condition given the clear childhood onset and lifelong trajectory. This presentation meets criteria for ADHD (combined type per history, coded as F90.0).
